### **1. Demand for platinum** 

- _After a decline in 2008, demand for platinum in 2009 is set for a heavy fall as global vehicle production contracts sharply, mainly in the developed economies.  Autocatalyst demand is unlikely to regain its 2008 level before 2012.  Meanwhile, although jewellery is expected to recover strongly in 2009 and thereafter trend higher, this benefit will be eroded by lower retail investment demand (2008 was exceptional) and weakness in other applications._ 

|**Platinum 000 ozs**|**2008**|**2009F**|**2010F**|**2011F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Autocatalyst|3,814|3,236|3,393|3,706|
|Jewellery|1,646|2,005|2,160|2,310|
|_Chemical_|346|383|368|393|

### **1.1  Autocatalyst** 

- Our estimates for autocatalyst demand have been scaled back over the forecast period, with a recovery to 2008 levels now unlikely to occur before 2012.  This In the main relates to lower estimates for European demand in 2010 and 2011 and a scaling back of demand in the “other regions” category from 2009.  We have also eased back our estimates for China. 

- On the whole, the driver of these changes is lower forecast vehicle production although we have also adjusted some of our assumptions of catalyst loadings following an in depth review in advance of our Platinum & Palladium Survey 2009. 

- **1.2 Jewellery** (now reported as gross fabrication, rather than net of scrap) 

- On the assumption that prices will remain supportive for platinum jewellery, especially in China, we

have raised our demand estimates over the forecast period starting with a forecast 2m ounces for 2009.  While the fundamentals suggest otherwise, the possibility of sharply higher prices and greater volatility is an ongoing risk for jewellery demand.  While not fundamentally based, such conditions may occur on a sharp rally in gold prices or perhaps a US listing of a platinum ETF (an application is currently under review). 

### **1.3 Industrial & other applications** 

- We remain of the view that retail investment will fall considerably in 2009 (after the record levels of 2008) and continue to trend lower thereafter.  Demand in industrial applications is expected to remain stable in overall terms with a slight underlying uptrend from 2010.

### **2. Demand for palladium** 

- _We now envisage a somewhat sharper decline in palladium demand in 2009, lead by downgrades in our forecast for autocatalyst, which extend over the forecast period. Although we have raised our estimates for jewellery demand, this provides only limited compensation and with other sectors remaining sluggish, we now visualise lower levels of overall demand than previously forecast – particularly in 2009 and 2010._ 

|**Palladium 000 ozs**|**2008**|**2009F**|**2010F**|**2011F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Autocatalyst|4,416|3,912|4,490|4,981|
|Jewellery|1,301|1,378|1,417|1,467|

|_Electronics_|1,347|1,192|1,310|1,466|
|_Retail investment_|84|105|70|45|
|_Other_|91|84|86|93|
|Industrial|2,683|2,398|2,481|2,675|
|**Total**|**8,399**|**7,688**|**8,388**|**9,123**|



### **2.1 Autocatalyst** 

- As with platinum, our forecast of demand for palladium in autocatalyst has suffered from scaled back estimates of vehicle production and in some areas, revised loading assumptions stemming from our major pre‐survey review.  On a regional basis, the areas most affected are Europe and our “other regions” segment which is primarily emerging markets (but excluding China). 

- Despite these changes, palladium is expected to fare better than platinum and recover its expected losses in 2009 during 2010.  This is underpinned by substitution gains in both gasoline and diesel, together with some improvement in vehicle production from 2010. 

- **2.2 Jewellery** (now reported as gross fabrication, rather than net of scrap) 

- We have raised our forecasts for jewellery fabrication following a somewhat better outcome in 2008 than anticipated.  However, palladium jewellery continues to labour with something of an identity complex in its principal market of China and we have therefore taken a cautious view of projected demand until this issue is addressed through coordinated marketing.  Although palladium continues to enjoy a considerable price advantage, its aspirational competitor platinum has become more affordable over recent months. 

### **2.3 Industrial** 

- In overall terms, our fore

casts in this area are largely unchanged, with weakness in chemicals largely offset by higher estimates for retail investment.

### **3. Supply** 

### **3.1  Platinum supply** 

- _We now include the recycling of old jewellery scrap as a component of supply (correspondingly, jewellery demand is reported on a gross fabrication basis).  Driven by record high prices, this was a major feature of platinum supply in 2008 but is expected to subside dramatically from 2009 onwards.  Aside from this, our estimates for mine production and autocatalyst recycling are essentially unchanged from our previous report._ 

|**Platinum 000 ozs**|**2008**|**2009F**|**2010F**|**2011F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Mineproduction:**|||||
|South Africa|4,671|4,709|4,948|5,231|
|Russia|835|779|772|758|
|Canada|227|192|268|276|
|United States|115|104|92|60|
|Zimbabwe|180|179|192|250|
|Others|123|113|110|116|
|**Total mineproduction**|**6,151**|**6,077**|**6,382**|**6,691**|
|Autocatalyst recycling|998|1,065|1,140|1,236|
|Jewelleryscrap|910|282|227|196|
|**Total supply**|**8,059**|**7,424**|**7,749**|**8,124**|



- Whilst failing to transform the economics of mining, improvements in PGM prices since the lows of October 2008 have reduced the potential attractiveness of wholesale production cuts by the majors in South Africa.  Meanwhile, their expansion projects remain on hold and we expect any easing of production this year to be modest and offset by the entry of new mines from the junior sector.  Adding support to our view that South African production will stabilise this year is that some key events of 2008 are unlikely to recur; namely the flooding of the Amandelbult mine and the five day industry wide stoppage in January last year amid the nation’s power crisis. 

- The record high prices of early 2008 triggered heavy outflows of old platinum jewellery scrap, mainly from Japan but with some contribution from China.  This lead to what we believe were record volumes of recycling from this source and a massive addition to supply, primarily over the first half of 2008.  Since then, volumes have fallen sharply and we visualise no repeat of this phenomenon over the forecast period.  However, the recognition of this as a separately identifiable component will result in a heavy fall in overall supply in 2009, even though the forecast decline in global mine production is relatively modest.

**Market Parameters Report – April 2009** 





### **3.2  Palladium supply** 

- _Apart from the addition of jewellery scrap, our forecast for Palladium supply remains largely unchanged over the forecast years._ 

|**Palladium 000 ozs**|**2008**|**2009F**|**2010F**|**2011F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Mineproduction:**|||||
|South Africa|2,366|2,659|2,845|3,036|
|Russia|2,712|2,520|2,520|2,520|
|Canada|524|282|369|373|
|United States|384|344|304|200|
|Zimbabwe|140|139|155|199|
|Others|255|250|245|219|
|**Total mineproducti

on**|**6,381**|**6,194**|**6,438**|**6,547**|
|Autocatalyst recycling|1,184|1,450|1,731|2,037|
|Jewelleryscrap|195|108|100|95|
|**Total supply**|**7,759**|**7,752**|**8,269**|**8,679**|



- We have made only minimal revisions to our forecasts of mine production and expect the moderate further decline of 2009 to be recovered in 2010.  Meanwhile, we are maintaining our estimates for autocatalyst recycling despite reports that flows have slowed in the face of lower PGM and steel prices.  Although we accept this is probably true, we believe the effects could be temporary with rising inventory levels being released into recycling later this year. In theory, this process should be aided by an injection of volume from the various “cash for clunkers” programmes which have emerged in Europe, most notably in Germany.  However, it remains to be seen how many of these vehicles will be physically scrapped as opposed to exported (unofficially) for use in less developed countries, a common theme of recent years. 

- Although less significant than for platinum, the recycling of palladium from old jewellery is a material component of supply; for example, this exceeded mine production in Zimbabwe last year.  However, this is expected to subside in 2009 and remain subdued over the remainder of the forecast period.

### **4. Market balances** 

### **4.1 Platinum** 

- _We are now estimating a moderate gross surplus for platinum in 2008 (previously a small deficit) and remain of the view that surplus conditions at the gross level will persist through to 2011.  Above‐ground stocks of platinum will rise as a result._ 

- _Given the strength of investment flows already this year, we have raised our estimate for ETF investment in 2009 and scaled back our assumptions for 2010 and 2011.  While inflows in 2009 already exceed 200,000 ounces, it remains to be seen as to how sustainable this will be over the course of this year and beyond._

### **4.2 Palladium** 

- _In comparison with our previous report, demand side revisions have had a notable effect on palladium’s underlying position in 2009 and 2010, when the market is now expected to be much closer to balance at the gross level.  Despite this, we continue to forecast a sizeable gross deficit for 2011._ 

- _Our forecasts for Russian government sales and ETF flows remain unchanged.  This produces a higher residual surplus in 2009 and 2010 and a balanced market in overall terms by 2011._

**5. Above‐ground stocks** 

- _Above‐ground stocks are implied from historical trade data for Switzerland (dating from 1970) and declared stocks on the Nymex and Tocom futures exchanges.  Excluded are stocks held by governments (including Russia), producers, refiners and fabricators and consumers._ 

|**Implied stocks**|**2008**|**2009F**|**2010F**|**2011F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Platinum:**|||||
|Stock atyear end(million ozs)|1.85|2.03|2.32|2.47|
|Demand cover(months)|2.8|3.4|3.7|3.7|
|**Palladium:**|||||
|Stock atyear end(million ozs)|7.67|8.74|8.37|7.67|
|Demand cover(months)|11.0|13.6|12.0|10.1|



- Over the next three years platinum’s demand cover is expected to rise from around 2.8 months to 3.7 months as its gross surplus persists. 

- For palladium, above‐ground stocks are forecast to remain substantial over the forecast period, with demand cover easing to approximately 10 months by 2011. 

- _Note: forecast sales of palladium from Russian state stocks have now been included as inflows to implied above‐ground stocks in Switzerland.  These inclusions serve to inflate stocks in Switzerland but are balanced by commensurate declines in Russia’s state owned inventories._ 

> **6. Prices and related indicators** 

Page | 6 

**Market Parameters Report – April 2009** 





### **6.1 Platinum** 

_Platinum encounters resistance at $1,200 and retreats to $1,100 territory.  Volatility ticks upward but remains subdued._ 

_As platinum reached $1,200, its RSI suggested over‐bought conditions, perhaps prompting its sell‐off, at least in part._ 

_With the 50 day and 200 day moving averages and the price having all intersected, this does not look especially supportive for platinum and may suggest the short‐term risk is to the downside._ 







Page | 7 

**Market Parameters Report – April 2009** 





### **6.2 Palladium** 

_Palladium has held its position above $200 despite weakness in platinum.  Volatility continues to trend lower suggesting some consolidation._ 

_The RSI appears mildly supportive, having retreated from over‐bought territory.  At least, there appears to be no immediate threat from this indicator._ 

_As with platinum, all points have now intersected which does not appear to be particularly supportive of prices at current levels._
